name: Tasmanian
world_status: statement found in an open source

earlier_scan.note: Retired code split into nine Tasmanian varieties; extinct, wordlist-level records only

new_statements.quote: The position of stress within a word is perhaps the most elusive aspect of Tasmanian phonology. We have the following source material: [a] Walker marks each vowel with either ¯ or ˘; these marks apparently indicate accent rather than quantity ... [c] Milligan says 'when a double consonant or two consonants stand together, the first carries the accent ...' ... [f] The 1972 Crowley recordings of Mrs. Heffernan and Mrs. Mundy. From these sources it appears that a disyllabic word is always stressed on the first syllable, whereas a trisyllabic word can be stressed on either first or second syllable. Our only general conclusion concerning stress in Tasmanian is thus: any syllable except the last can bear stress.
new_statements.citation: Crowley, Terry & R.M.W. Dixon. 1981. Tasmanian. In R.M.W. Dixon & Barry J. Blake (eds), Handbook of Australian Languages, Volume 2, pp. 394-421. Canberra: Australian National University Press.

new_statements.rule_in_words: From the fragmentary record (19th-c. accent diacritics, Milligan's remark, Tindale, the c.1900 Fanny Cochrane Smith cylinders and Crowley's 1972 recordings of rememberers): two-syllable words carry initial stress; three-syllable words may be stressed on the first or the second syllable; stress never falls on the final syllable. The authors decline to state a fixed position. (Vowel reduction to [ə] in unstressed syllables is noted on p. 412.)
new_statements.exceptions: None beyond the trisyllable variability; Milligan's 1859 remark is read as 'the vowel preceding a sequence of two consonants (in Milligan's orthography) bears stress'. Taylor 2006 (MA thesis, pp. 257-259) disputes the conclusion and argues the diacritics show near-uniform stress on the first word element (initial stress).
new_statements.domain_note: Word-level stress inferred from written records and a few late recordings of isolated words and songs; discussion 'based mainly on the mid-eastern and south-eastern languages' (Oyster Bay, South-East/Bruny Island) and assumed areally uniform across the island (p. 407). Languages extinct since the 19th c.; no phrase-level information.
new_statements.identity_note: tasm1247 is a Glottolog 'Bookkeeping' languoid for the retired ISO 639-3 code xtz 'Tasmanian' (split by CR 2019-047, effective 2020, into nine codes xpb, xpd, xpf, xph, xpl, xpv, xpw, xpx, xpz; Glottolog treats the Tasmanian languages as several small families, not one language). Crowley & Dixon 1981 describe 'the Tasmanian languages' collectively, stating that their phonology discussion is 'based mainly on the mid-eastern and south-eastern languages' (Oyster Bay, WALS 'toy' = Glottolog oyst1235; and South-Eastern/Bruny Island) and that phonetics/phonology appear areally uniform across the island. Any catalog entry should therefore be attached to the bookkeeping code only with this caveat, or re-keyed to Oyster Bay (oyst1235) / South-Eastern Tasmanian. Taylor 2006 uses the cover term 'Palawa' for the same corpus. Not to be confused with palawa kani (pala1356), the modern reconstructed language of the Tasmanian Aboriginal Centre.

sources.locator: Section 2.4 'Stress', p. 413 (pdf p. 434 of the ANU open-repository scan of HAL vol. 2)
sources.note: Dedicated section 2.4: stress position is 'the most elusive aspect of Tasmanian phonology'; from Walker's/Norman's accent marks, Milligan's remark, Tindale, the Fanny Cochrane Smith recordings and Crowley's 1972 recordings: disyllables always initial-stressed, trisyllables stressed on first or second syllable; only general conclusion: any syllable except the last can bear stress. Also (2.3, p.412) evidence for a central vowel [ə] in unstressed syllables.

sources.citation: Taylor, John Albert. 2006. The Palawa (Tasmanian Aboriginal) languages: a preliminary discussion. MA thesis, University of Tasmania. Section 7.9 'Stress and Accenting', pp. 257-259; section 7.3.3 'Marks to indicate stressing and accenting', p. 138.
sources.note: Quotes and disputes Crowley & Dixon 1981:413; argues from the 19th-c. diacritics (Walker, Sterling, G.A. Robinson, Cunningham) that 'in 99 per cent of word elements in initial position with vowels bearing these diacritics, the first vowel is marked with a bar', i.e. 'strong stressing of the first word element in words' (initial stress), with only infrequent stress on final word elements; applies Dixon's 'initial syllable is generally stressed' to Palawa but denies the alternating cadence.

sources.citation: Milligan, Joseph. 1859. On the dialects and language of the Aboriginal Tribes of Tasmania, and on their manners and customs. Papers and Proceedings of the Royal Society of Tasmania 3(2): 275-282 (orthography and accent remark, p. 282).
sources.note: Only: 'When a double consonant, or two consonants stand together, the first carries the accent, as in the English words cunningly, peppery, cobbler, pipkin.' (the primary remark Crowley & Dixon interpret as stress on the vowel preceding a CC sequence in his spelling).
